title: Undergraduate students: Guidelines to students on literature courses

paragraphs.text: While continuing the study of novels, short stories, and poetry which was begun in EL1, students on EL2 will also study dramatic texts. Hence it may be useful to make a couple of points about the reading of dramatic texts, to counter any temptation there might be to see them unfairly as inferior to other types of literature.

The first point, though it is perhaps an obvious one, can often be forgotten by students of literature who are reading a dramatic text rather than watching it at the theatre. It is the matter of performance. Dramatic texts are written not to stand alone, but to be used as scripts. The text makes a contribution – sometimes an extremely large one, at other times not so large – to a theatrical event which goes beyond what the script contains. So dramatic texts are 'completed' in performance. True, poems and novels may well call out for a kind of 'performance' too; but it differs from the type that playwrights have in mind. For their scripts to come into their own, playwrights assume a complex interrelation of factors: an audience of particular people who have come together to see a show; a stage with particular dimensions and facilities for the dramatist to exploit; actors who find apt characterisations for their roles and know how to communicate these with voice and physical movement; effective decor, costume and light; music perhaps; and, by no means least, the whole atmosphere and sense of occasion of a theatrical performance. None of these exist for the readers of play texts, and they must therefore build some sort of ‘Theatre of the Imagination' in their minds if the plays they read are to come to life.

In addition, given that one aspect of this course is to look at the drama produced in Britain between 1760 and 1935, another point comes into play, which is the historical development of the theatre during this period. This can be described under three main headings: the particular type of audience for which the plays were framed; the sort of theatrical 'apparatus' available to the playwright; and the type of drama which was produced.

If one looks at the development of drama over this period it can be seen that there were four distinct stages: Enlightenment Theatre (1760-1790), Romantic Theatre (1790-1840), Theatre of Ideas (1885-1915) and Modernist Theatre (1915-1935). The degree of change from one of these to the next under each of the headings mentioned above is worth pondering. With Enlightenment Theatre, on the whole it was the upper classes who went to the theatres, which were fairly small by today's standards and were lit by candles and oil-lamps, with scenery made of sliding boards and painted back-cloths. In these theatres, the new plays which established a strong reputation were mostly those known as 'comedies of manners', where verbal wit and complex intrigue were very much at a premium.

The audience for Romantic Theatre came from a wider social spectrum, swelled as it was by the increase in the size of the urban proletariat which went with the Industrial Revolution. Theatres grew larger, and increased in number. They were now better lit using gas and also limelight, and on the stage, the scenery grew more solid and elaborate than before. The most significant dramatic genre which grew up with all this change was 'melodrama'. The name was derived from the music - the ancestor of twentieth-century film-music - played between and with stretches of dialogue; but the name came to signify a kind of play which traded in simple, strong emotions and situations, and gave dialogue a lower place than spectacle in the hierarchy of theatrical elements. The plays dealt with popular themes of the time mysterious secrets and horrific events.

Jumping on a few decades, one arrives at the world of the late-nineteenth-century Theatre of Ideas. Here we encounter educated audiences who have a lively interest in current issues and new trends of thought, watching plays in theatres which were now lit by electric light. The stage was populated by naturalistic actors who, far from declaiming their speeches to the audience, appeared to take no notice at all of them, but just to go realistically about their business. Their aim was to depict modern life in a way that was 'photographically' as near a reflection as possible of the world outside the theatre.

The various sorts of Modernist Theatre which reacted against much of this in early-twentieth-century Britain diverged in several ways; but they had things in common. One of these was the expectation of small, but curious audiences (since the big audience would be elsewhere: at 'commercial' theatres, or watching movies and listening to radio). Small acting spaces - chamber theatres, theatre studios and even drawing rooms - were often the venue. Unlike late-nineteenth-century theatre, modernist theatre emphasised the theatrical, using song, dance, image projections and masks, in plays which called on ritual and fantasy and sometimes used the cultures of non-western sources in an effort to reveal areas of experience that previous drama, it was held, could not reach.
